info.event: Let’s start by identifying the trigger that caused these unpleasant emotions or thoughts. A trigger can be a significant event, a tiny occurrence, or even a single passing thought.
info.thought: An automatic thought arises in response to an event and triggers a wave of emotions. These can intensify and spawn new unhelpful thoughts, creating a vicious cycle. To stop it from growing, try to catch the automatic thought as early as possible and write it down.
info.body: Recall the moment the trigger occurred and pay attention to your bodily sensations. What specific physical reactions did you feel?
info.behavior: How did you behave after these emotions surfaced? What did you do, or perhaps, what did you avoid doing?
info.response: When you notice an automatic thought, it’s important to examine it closely. Often, these thoughts contain cognitive distortions. Your goal is to find a rational, more realistic response and form a helpful belief.
info.conclusion: Describe your conclusions: has your emotional state changed, how do you view the situation now, and what would you like to try differently next time?
info.comparison: Write down the arguments that support the automatic thought and those that contradict it. This will help you evaluate it objectively and see the situation from a broader perspective.

stepper.event: I made a mistake on a task at work
stepper.thought: I feel like I make mistakes often, and because of that, people treat me poorly
stepper.body: I felt my heart racing and a heaviness in my chest
stepper.behavior: I slammed the door and walked away
stepper.response: Everyone makes mistakes; it’s part of the work process. I can’t know what others are actually thinking, and my assumptions might be inaccurate
stepper.conclusion: If this happens again, I’ll try not to jump to conclusions about how others are reacting. I’ll also create a task checklist to boost my confidence and reduce the likelihood of similar mistakes

description: Turn journaling from a routine task into a creative and engaging process. Instead of just listing events, try telling the story of your day like a short narrative.
The AI assistant is here to support you: it will analyze your story and suggest the best way to fill in your journal by selecting the most appropriate categories and fields.
You can always edit or add to the AI’s suggestions to ensure your entry remains as personal and accurate as possible.
Your text will be saved in your journal, so it won’t disappear after the analysis and will always be available to you.
The AI makes working through your thoughts not only helpful but also inspiring, turning journaling into a space for self-expression and self-care.
hint: Describe the event, your feelings, and your thoughts. In your story, try to mention:
What emotions and physical sensations you experienced
Your adaptive response to the automatic thought
What conclusion you drew from the situation

automaticAnalysis.title: Recording emotions instead of thoughts
automaticAnalysis.description: You can’t disprove or change emotions themselves using an adaptive response. We log emotions separately; here, it’s important to capture the specific thought that triggered the feeling.
automaticAnalysis.right: I think I won’t be able to cope

automaticAnalysis.title: Too vague
automaticAnalysis.description: Sometimes a thought is recorded too broadly, making it hard to understand what exactly is causing the distress. It’s better to be specific.
automaticAnalysis.right: I think my colleagues view me as incompetent

automaticAnalysis.title: Recording facts instead of interpretations
automaticAnalysis.description: At this step, it’s important to reflect your interpretation of what happened, rather than the fact itself. We’ve already recorded the event earlier.
automaticAnalysis.right: Now my boss might think I’m irresponsible

automaticAnalysis.title: Complex or confusing phrasing
automaticAnalysis.description: It’s better to write down thoughts in simple, clear words. This makes it easier to formulate an adaptive, supportive response.
automaticAnalysis.wrong: I tend to believe that my opinion doesn’t matter
automaticAnalysis.right: My opinion doesn’t matter to anyone

automaticAnalysis.title: Skipping an automatic thought
automaticAnalysis.description: Sometimes it feels easier to jump straight to positive affirmations. But it’s important to first notice and record the automatic thought so you can work through it later.
automaticAnalysis.right: I’m not sure I can handle this

automaticAnalysis.title: Ignoring key thoughts
automaticAnalysis.description: Sometimes we only record milder thoughts to avoid the most painful ones. However, acknowledging key thoughts is what truly helps you understand yourself.
automaticAnalysis.wrong: I’m a little anxious about the future

smer.h2: Identify the link to your automatic thoughts
texts: Intermediate beliefs are the rules and assumptions through which we perceive the world around us.
When these beliefs become distorted, they can trigger automatic thoughts—often harsh and self-critical.
In this section, you can connect your beliefs and automatic thoughts to understand them more deeply and begin working toward change.
